abstract: Summary The liver is frequently affected by metastasis in colorectal cancer patients; however, the precise interaction between the liver microenvironment and metastatic colorectal cancer cells remains elusive. Our study revealed that NID1, present in extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from metastatic colorectal cancer, plays a pivotal role in promoting colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM). EV-NID1 facilitates epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in colorectal cancer cells by modulating EMT-associated genes. Moreover, EV-NID1 activates hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), which in turn stimulate neutrophil infiltration and induce the formation of neutrophil-trapping networks (NETs) within the hepatic metastatic microenvironment via interleukin-11 (IL-11) secretion. This process ultimately reshapes the tumor microenvironment (TME) and fosters the establishment of a metastatic niche conducive to CRLM. Notably, targeted inhibition of IL-11 signaling via anti-IL-11 monoclonal antibodies effectively suppressed EV-NID1-induced liver metastasis in a murine model. In summary, our findings elucidate the mechanism underlying EV-NID1-mediated regulation of CRLM, identifying a promising therapeutic target for intervention in this disease.

Experimental model and study participant details
Serum collection
The primary cohort comprised 20 healthy donors and 70 CRC patients who underwent radical surgery at the 2nd Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University from January 2021 to April 2023. Fresh serum was obtained during surgery. Written consent was obtained from all patients before bile or serum collection.
CRC cohort and ethics
The primary CRC cohort consisted of patients who underwent surgical resection at the Cancer Hospital Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences from 2010 to 2018. Among them, 174 CRC patients were selected from the primary cohort if they met the following criteria: (I) underwent radical resection; (II) had formalin-immobilized tumor tissues, followed up, and had a complete medical history; (III) survived more than 30 days after surgery; and (IV) had no other malignancies. Tumor tissues were staged and classified according to the 8th edition AJCC/UICC TNM classification system. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Shanxi Provincial Cancer Hospital/Shanxi Hospital of the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences Cancer Hospital.
Cells and reagents
The human CRC cell lines SW480, KM12 and HCT116, the human colonic epithelial cell line NCM-460 and the hepatic stellate cell line LX-2 were obtained from the Chinese Academy of Sciences Cell Bank (Shanghai, China), authenticated by STR analysis and tested for mycoplasma contamination. SW480, HCT116 and KM12 cells were maintained in RPMI 1640 medium (Thermo Fisher), NCM-460 cells were maintained in DMEM/F-12 medium (Gibco) and LX-2 cells were maintained in MEM (Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Thermo Fisher) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin under 5% CO2 at 37°C.
In vivo
experiments
All the animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences (NCC2023A355). Six-week-old female BALB/c mice were purchased from Gempharmatech Laboratory (Nanjing, China). For spleen injection, after anesthesia, the spleens of the mice were removed via laparotomy. For the spleen injection, 2.5 × 106 CRC cells suspended in 50 μL of PBS were injected into the distal tip of the spleen with an insulin syringe (BD, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). A whitening bulge of the spleen was observed in the injection area. After the whitening bulge disappeared, the spleen was removed after ligation of the splenic vessels, and the abdominal wound was then sutured. The animals were maintained until death or until the end of the experiment. For intracardiac injections, the preparations used were similar to those used for splenic injections. After anesthesia, the location of the mouse heart was localized, 50 μL of PBS-suspended CRC cells were injected into the interior of the cardiac chambers using an insulin syringe, and arterial blood was withdrawn back to the heart prior to the injection to indicate the correct location. For cecum injection, 1 × 106 CRC cells suspended in 50 μL of matrix gel (Corning) dilution (matrix gel: PBS = 4:1) were injected into the plasma membrane layer of the cecum using an insulin syringe (BD, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). A whitening and bulging of the cecum was observed in the injection area upon successful injection, and then the abdominal wound was sutured. The animals were maintained until death or until the end of the experiment. A live imaging system (IVIS Spectrum; PerkinElmer) was used to detect
in vivo
metastases. Liver metastases were counted and confirmed by H&E staining.
For EV treatment, the mice were i.p. injected with 15 μg of EVs or with PBS as a control once per week for 3 weeks. For cilengitide and anti-IL-11 antibody treatment, the mice were i.p. injected with cilengitide (75 mg/kg, 5 times/week, HY-16141, Master of Bioactive Molecules) and an anti-IL-11 antibody (25 μg per mouse, MAB218, R&D Systems) every other day.
Stable clones of SW480 cells (5 × 106 cells) or SW480 cells (5 × 106 cells) overexpressing NID1 were injected subcutaneously into nude mice. Beginning on the third day after tumor cell injection, if necessary, EVs or cilengitide (75 mg/kg, 5 times/week) were injected every 3 days via intraperitoneal injection. Tumor diameters were measured with an external caliper every 3 days. The tumor volume (V) was calculated according to the following formula: volume (mm3) = (length×width2)/2. After 18/21 days, the tumors were removed, photographed and weighed.
Ethical statement
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences. This study was conducted following the International Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research Involving Human Subjects (CIOMS) and approved by the Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences.
Method details
Exosome isolation
Exosomes were isolated from serum and CRC medium via differential centrifugation. In brief, serum and Exo-depleted–fetal bovine serum media were centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 30 min at 4°C. The impurities, cellular sediment, and debris were removed, and the supernatant was ultracentrifuged at 110,000 × g for 70 min at 4°C. After that, the pellets were resuspended in PBS and ultracentrifuged again at 110,000 × g for 70 min at 4°C. The final pellets, which were mainly Exosomes, were resuspended and resuspended in PBS.
Patient-derived organoids
Freshly resected CRC tissues were minced into 0.5–1 mm3 pieces. The supernatants, including any blood cells and floating pieces of fat, were discarded. After incubation in IV collagenase (Sigma‒Aldrich) for 30 min, the tissues were passed through 70-μm filter gauze and centrifuged at 300 × g for 5 min at 4°C. After the removal of the supernatant, Matrigel (R&D, Minnesota, USA) and expansion medium were proportionally mixed with the pellets and seeded in 24-well plates. The organoids were incubated for 10–15 days in Bowel cancer organoid medium (Mogengel Biotechnology) supplemented with 1% penicillin/streptomycin.The collection of all samples was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University (Approval No. KY2024-176).
Tissue microarray and IHC
Typical paraffin-embedded sections of CRC tissues were used for TMA construction and immunohistochemistry (IHC) scoring after hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining to confirm the histological features of all samples by a senior pathologist. For the TMA construct, a 1.5 mm diameter core biopsy sample was extracted from each.
Sample and placed on a TMA slide
For IHC, slides were pretreated in EDTA buffer (pH 9.0) or sodium citrate buffer (pH 6.0) for antigen retrieval. Primary anti-PTPN9 antibody (1:50), anti-
p
-FGFR2 antibody (1:100) and anti-ACAP1 antibody (1:100) were used and incubated at 4°C overnight. Rabbit anti-goat and goat anti-rabbit antibodies labeled with biotin (Zsbio, Beijing, China) were used at room temperature for 30 min. The peroxidase reaction was carried out with 3,3′-diaminobenzidine solution (Coolaber).
The stained slides were screened with a slide scanner (Pannoramic MIDI; 3DHISTECH, Budapest, Hungary). The tumor area was selected by senior pathologists, and the IHC results were quantified using Quant Center software. The area of each area of staining was calculated, and the staining intensity was classified as weak, medium, or strong. IHC score = (percentage of weak intensity×1) + (percentage of medium intensity×2) + (percentage of strong intensity×3). The cohort was divided into different groups on the basis of the cutoff value of the IHC score, which was identified as the point where the sum of specificity and sensitivity was the highest in the receiver operating characteristic curve.
PKH67 fluorescent labeling
Purified exosomes were labeled with PKH67 fluorescence (Sigma). Exosomes were resuspended in 100 μL of diluent C and then mixed with 100 μL of diluent C containing 5 μL of PKH67 dye solution (4 × 10−6M). After PKH67 staining, the exosomes were washed in PBS and collected by ultracentrifugation (110,000 × g for 70 min) at 4°C to remove the free dye.
Transmission electron microscopy
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was used to observe exosome morphology. The purified exosomes were dropped on a copper grid and observed via transmission electron microscopy (FEI Tecnai Spirit TEM T12, Thermo Scientific) at 80 kV.
Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and NanoFCM
The exosome particle size was measured via nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) using a ZetaView PMX 110 (Particle Metrix, Meerbusch, Germany), and nanoflow was measured using N30E (NanoFCM, Xiamen, China). The purified exosomes were diluted 1:200 in PBS and subjected to NTA or NanoFCM. Each sample was measured in triplicate. Exosome numbers and size distributions were analyzed using Zetaview.
Cell proliferation assay
CCK-8 assays were performed to assess cell proliferation. Briefly, the cells were plated into 96-well plates (3 × 103 cells/well) and incubated for 4 days. A total of 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent (Dojindo, Kumamoto, Japan) was added each day, and the mixture was incubated at 37°C for 1 h. The absorbance value at 450 nm was detected using a spectrophotometer (Molecular Devices Company, France).
Transwell assay
To detect changes in cell migration and invasion, a transwell assay was performed using 24-well plates with chambers (Corning Inc., 8.0-μm pore size) with/without Matrigel precoating. A total of 5 × 104 SW480 cells or 1 × 105 KM12 cells were seeded into the upper chambers (diluted 1:6 with serum-free medium). Approximately 500 μL of complete medium supplemented with 20% FBS was added to the lower chamber. After incubation for 24 h, the cells on the lower side of the chamber were fixed with methanol and stained with 0.5% crystal violet (Solarbio) for 30 min. The cells were counted in three random fields at 200× magnification.
Mass spectrometry
Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC‒MS/MS) was performed by OEbiotech Company. On-line chromatographic separation was performed on an Easy nLC 1200 system (Thermo Fisher). Data Related Acquisition (DDA) MS was used to collect series of MS data on a ThermoFisher Q Exactive mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher, USA) equipped with a Nano-Flex ion source.
RNA sequencing
Total mRNA was extracted from SW480, SW480-LM3 and LX-2 cells using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen). The RNA was sequenced via an Illumina HiSeq 4000 (LC-Bio Technologies). Clean reads were separately aligned to the reference genome in orientation mode using TopHat software. The sequence reads were mapped to the reference genome using HISAT2 software. The transcript abundances (read counts) were estimated with StringTie. Normalization and differential expression analysis of mRNAs were conducted using DESeq2 in the R package.
Quantitative real-time PCR
TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) was used to separate total mRNA from frozen CRC cell lines according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The RNA quality was subsequently determined via a NanoDrop system (Thermo Fisher). The purified RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using a high-capacity cDNA reverse transcription kit (TOYOBO, Japan), and RT‒qPCR was performed using SYBR Green master mix (Roche, Switzerland). The relative expression levels of the target genes were calculated using the 2-ΔΔCt method, and GAPDH was used as an internal control. All primers were designed using Primer Express version 5.0 software (Applied Biosystems, USA).
Immunofluorescence assay
The cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min and incubated in Tween 20 for cell membrane perforation. The cells were incubated in 5% goat serum to block nonspecific antigen binding for 30 min and then incubated with primary antibodies against NID1 (1:100), IL-11 (1:100) and Destin (1:100) for 12 h at 4°C. The secondary antibodies goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 594 (Invitrogen, Cat # A-21207) and anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 488 (Invitrogen, Cat # A-21202) were used to immerse the cells for 1 h at room temperature. Nuclei were stained with DAPI (Thermo Fisher), and images were taken with a confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss, LSM880). The Pearson coefficient was analyzed with Image-Pro Plus.
Immunofluorescence of paraffin-embedded tissues
Immunofluorescence (IF) staining was performed as previously described.

After antigen retrieval and antigen blocking, the sections were incubated with diluted primary antibodies against MPO (1:50), H3Cit (1:200), and IL-11 (1:100) at 4°C overnight. The sections were subsequently incubated with CY3- or FITC-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:2,000, Thermo Fisher Scientific) at room temperature for 2 h. Finally, the sections were mounted in anti-fade mounting medium with DAPI (Beyotime). The levels of NETs were evaluated as described above.
Western blotting
Total protein was extracted using radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) lysis buffer (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) supplemented with 1% PMSF (Beyotime) and 1% phosphatase inhibitor (Solarbio, Beijing, China). Proteins were separated via 10% SDS‒PAGE after denaturation and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. Primary antibodies against CD63 (1:1,000), TSG-101 (1:1,000), calnexin (1:1,000), NID1 (1:1,000), E-cadherin (1:1,000), N-cadherin (1:1,000), Snail (1:1,000), vimentin (1:1,000), ZEB1 (1:1,000), and IL-11 (1:1,000) and corresponding secondary antibodies were used. The signal was detected via enhanced chemiluminescence (Millipore).
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
The IL-6, IL-8, IL-11 and TIMP2 concentrations in the LX-2 culture medium were measured by ELISA using the hIL-6 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04638h), hIL-8 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04641h), hIL-11 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04596h) and TIMP2 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04733h) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The ELISA absorbance values were read on a BIOTEK spectrophotometer (Vermont, USA) at 450 nm.
Construction of the NID1 expression plasmid
To increase the expression level of NID1, we amplified the human NID1 gene from cDNA by PCR and cloned it into the pLenti-EF1a lentiviral vector (GeneChem, China). In addition, to express NID1 in cellular EVs, the NID1 fragment was cloned and inserted into the CMV-XP-MCS-EF1-Puro cloning lentiviral vector (System Biosciences) using XPack EV Protein Engineering Technology (System Biosciences). NID1 was expressed through XPack EV Protein Engineering Technology (System Biosciences) for expression in the EVs of HCT116 and NCM-460 cells. The extracellular vesicle (EV) purification process was performed as described above. The purified EV-NID1 and control EVs were resuspended in Exo-depleted–fetal bovine serum media for further use. To inhibit exosome secretion, donor cells were treated with GW4869 (MedChemExpress) for 48 h. The conditioned medium was then collected, and EVs were isolated using the ultracentrifugation method described above. The GW4869-treated EV fraction was subsequently incubated with recipient colorectal cancer cells under the same conditions.
Overexpression and knockdown
To increase the expression level of NID1, the human NID1 gene was amplified from cDNA via PCR and subsequently cloned and inserted into the pcDNA3.1 or pLenti-EF1a lentiviral vector (GeneChem, China). Short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) and the packaging plasmids GV, pHelper1.0 and pHelper2.0 were used for knockdown.
Cytokine antibody array
Cytokines were detected in the media of LX-2 cells stimulated with EV-NID1 using the Human Inflammation Array C3 Kit (AAH-INF-3-2, RayBiotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, LX-2 cells were stimulated with EV-NID1 for 72 h. The culture supernatants were collected, centrifuged at 1,000 × g to discard the pellets and 10 × concentrated with Amicon Ultra15 mL filters (10 kDa, Millipore) at 4,000 × g. Array membranes, previously spotted with capture antibodies by the manufacturer, were incubated with 1 mL of culture supernatants overnight at 4°C. After being washed three times, the membranes were incubated with streptavidin-HRP for 30 min and visualized with Chemi-Reagent Mix. The protein signal was detected with a chemifluorescence detection system (Amersham Imager 600, GE). Quantitative analysis of specific protein expression was performed using ImageJ.

Quantification and statistical analysis
Statistical analysis
SPSS 22.0 (IBM, Chicago, Illinois, USA) and GraphPad Prism 6.0 (GraphPad Software, CA, USA) were used for statistical analysis. The correlations between NID1 expression and clinicopathological features were evaluated via the chi-square test. The Kaplan‒Meier method was used to plot survival curves, and the log rank test was used to analyze the statistical significance. The “survival” R package in RStudio software was used to calculate Harrell’s concordance index (C-index), which measures the proportion of pairs for which the predicted and observed outcomes are concordant. Multivariate analysis with a Cox regression model was performed to compare independent prognostic factors. A paired
t
test was used for the comparison of two paired groups, and one-way or two-way ANOVA was performed to analyze the differences among multiple groups.

Rabbit anti-goat and goat anti-rabbit antibodies labeled with biotin (Zsbio, Beijing, China) were used at room temperature for 30 min. The peroxidase reaction was carried out with 3,3′-diaminobenzidine solution (Coolaber).
The stained slides were screened with a slide scanner (Pannoramic MIDI; 3DHISTECH, Budapest, Hungary). The tumor area was selected by senior pathologists, and the IHC results were quantified using Quant Center software. The area of each area of staining was calculated, and the staining intensity was classified as weak, medium, or strong. IHC score = (percentage of weak intensity×1) + (percentage of medium intensity×2) + (percentage of strong intensity×3). The cohort was divided into different groups on the basis of the cutoff value of the IHC score, which was identified as the point where the sum of specificity and sensitivity was the highest in the receiver operating characteristic curve.
PKH67 fluorescent labeling
Purified exosomes were labeled with PKH67 fluorescence (Sigma). Exosomes were resuspended in 100 μL of diluent C and then mixed with 100 μL of diluent C containing 5 μL of PKH67 dye solution (4 × 10−6M). After PKH67 staining, the exosomes were washed in PBS and collected by ultracentrifugation (110,000 × g for 70 min) at 4°C to remove the free dye.
Transmission electron microscopy
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was used to observe exosome morphology. The purified exosomes were dropped on a copper grid and observed via transmission electron microscopy (FEI Tecnai Spirit TEM T12, Thermo Scientific) at 80 kV.
Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and NanoFCM
The exosome particle size was measured via nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) using a ZetaView PMX 110 (Particle Metrix, Meerbusch, Germany), and nanoflow was measured using N30E (NanoFCM, Xiamen, China). The purified exosomes were diluted 1:200 in PBS and subjected to NTA or NanoFCM. Each sample was measured in triplicate. Exosome numbers and size distributions were analyzed using Zetaview.
Cell proliferation assay
CCK-8 assays were performed to assess cell proliferation. Briefly, the cells were plated into 96-well plates (3 × 103 cells/well) and incubated for 4 days. A total of 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent (Dojindo, Kumamoto, Japan) was added each day, and the mixture was incubated at 37°C for 1 h. The absorbance value at 450 nm was detected using a spectrophotometer (Molecular Devices Company, France).
Transwell assay
To detect changes in cell migration and invasion, a transwell assay was performed using 24-well plates with chambers (Corning Inc., 8.0-μm pore size) with/without Matrigel precoating. A total of 5 × 104 SW480 cells or 1 × 105 KM12 cells were seeded into the upper chambers (diluted 1:6 with serum-free medium). Approximately 500 μL of complete medium supplemented with 20% FBS was added to the lower chamber. After incubation for 24 h, the cells on the lower side of the chamber were fixed with methanol and stained with 0.5% crystal violet (Solarbio) for 30 min. The cells were counted in three random fields at 200× magnification.
Mass spectrometry
Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC‒MS/MS) was performed by OEbiotech Company. On-line chromatographic separation was performed on an Easy nLC 1200 system (Thermo Fisher). Data Related Acquisition (DDA) MS was used to collect series of MS data on a ThermoFisher Q Exactive mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher, USA) equipped with a Nano-Flex ion source.
RNA sequencing
Total mRNA was extracted from SW480, SW480-LM3 and LX-2 cells using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen). The RNA was sequenced via an Illumina HiSeq 4000 (LC-Bio Technologies). Clean reads were separately aligned to the reference genome in orientation mode using TopHat software. The sequence reads were mapped to the reference genome using HISAT2 software. The transcript abundances (read counts) were estimated with StringTie. Normalization and differential expression analysis of mRNAs were conducted using DESeq2 in the R package.
Quantitative real-time PCR
TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) was used to separate total mRNA from frozen CRC cell lines according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The RNA quality was subsequently determined via a NanoDrop system (Thermo Fisher). The purified RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using a high-capacity cDNA reverse transcription kit (TOYOBO, Japan), and RT‒qPCR was performed using SYBR Green master mix (Roche, Switzerland). The relative expression levels of the target genes were calculated using the 2-ΔΔCt method, and GAPDH was used as an internal control. All primers were designed using Primer Express version 5.0 software (Applied Biosystems, USA).
Immunofluorescence assay
The cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min and incubated in Tween 20 for cell membrane perforation. The cells were incubated in 5% goat serum to block nonspecific antigen binding for 30 min and then incubated with primary antibodies against NID1 (1:100), IL-11 (1:100) and Destin (1:100) for 12 h at 4°C. The secondary antibodies goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 594 (Invitrogen, Cat # A-21207) and anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 488 (Invitrogen, Cat # A-21202) were used to immerse the cells for 1 h at room temperature. Nuclei were stained with DAPI (Thermo Fisher), and images were taken with a confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss, LSM880). The Pearson coefficient was analyzed with Image-Pro Plus.
Immunofluorescence of paraffin-embedded tissues
Immunofluorescence (IF) staining was performed as previously described.
63
After antigen retrieval and antigen blocking, the sections were incubated with diluted primary antibodies against MPO (1:50), H3Cit (1:200), and IL-11 (1:100) at 4°C overnight. The sections were subsequently incubated with CY3- or FITC-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:2,000, Thermo Fisher Scientific) at room temperature for 2 h. Finally, the sections were mounted in anti-fade mounting medium with DAPI (Beyotime). The levels of NETs were evaluated as described above.
Western blotting
Total protein was extracted using radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) lysis buffer (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) supplemented with 1% PMSF (Beyotime) and 1% phosphatase inhibitor (Solarbio, Beijing, China). Proteins were separated via 10% SDS‒PAGE after denaturation and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. Primary antibodies against CD63 (1:1,000), TSG-101 (1:1,000), calnexin (1:1,000), NID1 (1:1,000), E-cadherin (1:1,000), N-cadherin (1:1,000), Snail (1:1,000), vimentin (1:1,000), ZEB1 (1:1,000), and IL-11 (1:1,000) and corresponding secondary antibodies were used. The signal was detected via enhanced chemiluminescence (Millipore).
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
The IL-6, IL-8, IL-11 and TIMP2 concentrations in the LX-2 culture medium were measured by ELISA using the hIL-6 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04638h), hIL-8 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04641h), hIL-11 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04596h) and TIMP2 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04733h) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The ELISA absorbance values were read on a BIOTEK spectrophotometer (Vermont, USA) at 450 nm.
Construction of the NID1 expression plasmid
To increase the expression level of NID1, we amplified the human NID1 gene from cDNA by PCR and cloned it into the pLenti-EF1a lentiviral vector (GeneChem, China). In addition, to express NID1 in cellular EVs, the NID1 fragment was cloned and inserted into the CMV-XP-MCS-EF1-Puro cloning lentiviral vector (System Biosciences) using XPack EV Protein Engineering Technology (System Biosciences). NID1 was expressed through XPack EV Protein Engineering Technology (System Biosciences) for expression in the EVs of HCT116 and NCM-460 cells. The extracellular vesicle (EV) purification process was performed as described above. The purified EV-NID1 and control EVs were resuspended in Exo-depleted–fetal bovine serum media for further use. To inhibit exosome secretion, donor cells were treated with GW4869 (MedChemExpress) for 48 h. The conditioned medium was then collected, and EVs were isolated using the ultracentrifugation method described above. The GW4869-treated EV fraction was subsequently incubated with recipient colorectal cancer cells under the same conditions.
Overexpression and knockdown
To increase the expression level of NID1, the human NID1 gene was amplified from cDNA via PCR and subsequently cloned and inserted into the pcDNA3.1 or pLenti-EF1a lentiviral vector (GeneChem, China). Short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) and the packaging plasmids GV, pHelper1.0 and pHelper2.0 were used for knockdown.
Cytokine antibody array
Cytokines were detected in the media of LX-2 cells stimulated with EV-NID1 using the Human Inflammation Array C3 Kit (AAH-INF-3-2, RayBiotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, LX-2 cells were stimulated with EV-NID1 for 72 h. The culture supernatants were collected, centrifuged at 1,000 × g to discard the pellets and 10 × concentrated with Amicon Ultra15 mL filters (10 kDa, Millipore) at 4,000 × g. Array membranes, previously spotted with capture antibodies by the manufacturer, were incubated with 1 mL of culture supernatants overnight at 4°C. After being washed three times, the membranes were incubated with streptavidin-HRP for 30 min and visualized with Chemi-Reagent Mix. The protein signal was detected with a chemifluorescence detection system (Amersham Imager 600, GE). Quantitative analysis of specific protein expression was performed using ImageJ.
Bioinformatics analysis of public datasets
All public CRC patient datasets used in this study are described in
Figure S2
C. Expression and clinical data of the TCGA rectal adenocarcinoma (READ) and colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) cohorts were obtained from the MD Anderson standardized data browser (
http://bioinformatics.mdanderson.org/TCGA/databrowser/
). For the analyses, the RNA-Seq by Expectation Maximization (RSEM)-normalized expression values from the Illumina RNASeqV2 (genes) datasets were used. Clinical and expression data from other CRC patient datasets were downloaded from NCBI GEO (
www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo
). The differential expression between tumors and adjacent normal colon tissue samples was calculated via paired t tests. The hazard ratio and significance for survival analysis were calculated using the log rank test. The Survminer R package (
https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=survminer
) was used to determine optimal cutoff values for the binary classification of cases (high/low expression).

Introduction
Colorectal cancer (CRC) ranks as the second leading cause of cancer-related death globally, with liver metastases accounting for approximately 50% of CRC-related fatalities.
1
Despite advancements in surgical and systemic therapies, patients with colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLMs) continue to face a grim prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 15%, presenting a significant clinical challenge.
2
,
3
Hepatic resection remains the sole option for long-term survival; however, more than 80% of patients are deemed ineligible for surgery upon diagnosis.
4
,
5
The interplay between tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in CRC liver metastasis. Tumor cells orchestrate the formation of a premetastatic niche within the TME, facilitating distant metastasis.
6
,
7
Extracellular vesicles (EVs), which carry a cargo of lipids, proteins, and RNAs that modulate recipient cell behavior, have emerged as vital mediators of intercellular communication.
8
,
9
,
10
Tumor-derived exosomes have been implicated in shaping premetastatic niches, fostering the survival and proliferation of disseminated tumor cells in distant organs.
11
,
12
,
13
,
14
Hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) undergo a phenotypic switch from a quiescent to a highly proliferative and motile state, influencing CRC cell behavior through extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling.
15
,
16
Activated hepatic stellate cells (α-HSCs) are pivotal in both primary and secondary liver tumors, underscoring the importance of exploring CRC-HSC interactions in CRLM pathogenesis.
17
,
18
Recent investigations have highlighted the role of the exosomal protein NID1 in hepatocellular carcinoma metastasis, which modulates the TME by influencing various cell types, including tumor cells and fibroblasts.
19
,
20
Furthermore, EVs released by chronic lymphocytic leukemia cells can reprogram cancer-associated fibroblasts, nurturing the TME.
21
HSCs play a crucial role in tumor metastatic progression and facilitate CRC cell recruitment during CRLM development by orchestrating premetastatic niche formation.
22
In this study, we discovered that highly metastatic CRC cells secrete NID1-enriched EVs, which promote liver metastasis by modulating CRC cell behavior and activating HSCs, thereby altering the TME. These findings offer a biomarker for CRLM and a potential strategy for predicting the risk of CRC-driven secondary liver cancer.
Results
Establishment and characterization of metastatic CRC cells
To increase the metastatic potential to the liver, we used an
in vivo
selection process to isolate highly liver metastatic CRC cells from both SW480 and KM12 parental cell lines. SW480/KM12 cells were injected into the spleens of Nude mice to mimic CRLM. After 2 weeks, the mice were euthanized, and their livers were dissected to isolate tumor tissues. These tissues were then treated with digestive enzymes to obtain single-cell suspensions, which were subsequently cultured. Once stabilized in culture, the purified cells, designated SW480/KM12-LM1, were reimplanted into the spleens of nude mice. Following another 2-week period, tumor tissue from the metastatic lesions in the liver was again excised, digested, cultured, and injected into the spleens of subsequent recipient mice. This process was repeated three times, as depicted in
Figure 1
A. After three rounds of
in vivo
screening, a highly metastatic colon cancer cell line named SW480/KM12-LM3 was established, and the hepatic metastatic efficiency of this cell line is illustrated in
Figures 1
B and 1C. Furthermore, the histopathology of liver metastases in LM3-implanted mice was analyzed by staining formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded sections with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), as shown in
Figure S1
A. Compared with those of the previous two generations, quantitative analysis of small animal live imaging and the number of liver nodules revealed a significant increase.

Cell supernatants from Exo-depleted-fetal bovine serum medium cultures were collected and subjected to ultracentrifugation to isolate Exos, which were then characterized through biomarker detection, transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and NanoFCM (

EV- NID1 contributes to CRLM
To elucidate the specific mechanism by which EV-NID1 influences CRC progression, we initially incubated organoids or CRC cells with PKH67-labeled X-Pack and XP-NID1 exosomes, which demonstrated the uptake of cell-secreted exosomes by the organoids and cells (
Figures S3
C and S3D). Subsequently, transwell experiments were performed on cells that had taken up exosomes. The results revealed that cells that received EV-NID1 exhibited increased metastatic capacities. We treated CRC cells with purified EV-NID1 and observed that EV-NID1 significantly enhanced their metastatic capacity. Furthermore, when exosome secretion was inhibited in donor cells using GW4869, the extracted fraction failed to promote CRC cell metastasis, effectively reversing the pro-metastatic effect of EV-NID1. These findings suggest that EV-NID1 plays a crucial role in promoting the metastatic potential of CRC cells (
Figures 4
A, 4B, and
S3
E). In addition, we investigated the role of endogenous NID1 and explored the metastatic and invasive capabilities of NID1 in tumor cells. C, 4D, and

E).

The exosomal protein NID1 induces the formation of a neutrophil-trapping network by promoting IL-11 secretion from HSCs
As evidenced by previous results, the EV treatment model demonstrated a positive effect of EV-NID1 on the distant metastasis of CRC cells, with the intervention of reducing EV-NID1 in mice reversing this effect. These findings strongly support the crucial role of EV-NID1 in CRLM. While the role of EV-NID1 in regulating EMT in tumor cells has been previously explored, it is important to consider the concept of a premetastatic ecological niche that prepares a favorable microenvironment for the survival and growth of distant metastatic cells. Previous studies have shown that EV-NID1 can be taken up by fibroblasts, altering their cellular functions.
19
Given that HSCs are activated during liver metastasis and can actively participate in CRLM,
32
we aimed to investigate the role of EV-NID1 in this context.
To explore the impact of EV-NID1 on CRLM, we incubated the human HSC line LX-2 with exosomes. The immunofluorescence results confirmed the uptake of exosomes, including EV-X-Pack and EV-XP-NID1, by LX-2 cells (
Figure 6

Subsequently, mRNA-seq analysis of LX-2 cells after incubation with EV-X-Pack or EV-XP-NID1 revealed the activation of multiple signaling pathways, including the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, neutrophil-trapping network (NET), and cytokine and cytokine receptor signaling pathways, as indicated by KEGG analysis (
Figure 6
B). On the basis of these findings, we conducted immunofluorescence assays on the livers of mice inoculated with tumor cells after receiving EV-X-Pack or EV-XP-NID1, which revealed a significant increase in NETs in the liver metastases of the mice receiving EV-XP-NID1 compared with those receiving EV-X-Pack (
Figure 6

Furthermore, we characterized the cytokines secreted by EV-NID1-stimulated HSCs by examining the expression of cytokines using cytokine arrays. This analysis identified interleukin (IL)-11 as a candidate cytokine involved in regulating the TME (
Figure 6

Figure 6

To elucidate the role of IL-11 in mediating NET formation, we established a mouse model (

Consistent with previous results, mice receiving EV-XP-NID1 developed more severe liver metastases than those receiving EV-X-Pack. However, treatment with anti-IL-11 antibodies reversed the ability of EV-NID1 to enhance liver metastasis (

Immunofluorescence experiments on the livers of the mice at the end of the experiment revealed a significant increase in NETs in the liver metastases of the mice that received EV-XP-NID1 compared with those that received EV-X-Pack. Notably, concurrent inhibition of IL-11 with an anti-IL-11 antibody led to a significant decrease in the number of NETs in the metastases (
Figure 7

Figure S5
C). Fluorescence images showed that EV-NID1-treated HSC-CM significantly enhanced CRC liver metastasis, suggesting a pro-metastatic role of EV-NID1 in the TME (
Figure S5
D). Immunofluorescence analysis further revealed that, by day 7 (before tumor cell implantation), IL-11 expression was markedly elevated in the liver of EV-NID1-treated mice (
Figure S5
E). By day 17 (metastatic nodule formation), a large presence of NETs was observed within liver metastatic lesions in the EV-NID1 group, suggesting that IL-11 contributes to neutrophil recruitment and NET formation (
Figure S5
F). Meanwhile, to determine the source of IL-11 and verify whether it is secreted by HSCs rather than highly metastatic CRC cells, we conducted ELISA and qPCR analyses to compare IL-11 expression levels in parental CRC cells, highly metastatic CRC cells (LM3), and LX-2 cells following EV-NID1 treatment. The results showed that LX-2 cells exhibited a significant increase in IL-11 expression and secretion upon EV-NID1 stimulation, confirming that IL-11 is primarily derived from HSCs. In contrast, IL-11 expression in tumor cells remained unchanged regardless of EV-NID1 treatment, suggesting that CRC cells themselves are not a major source of IL-11 (
Figures S5
G and S5H). These findings confirm that HSC-derived IL-11 promotes NET formation, which in turn facilitates CRC colonization and liver metastasis, further supporting the proposed mechanism.
These results further confirm the relationship between EV-NID1 and IL-11, indicating that IL-11 secreted by HSCs promotes the formation of NETs. Moreover, the use of an anti-IL-11 antibody effectively prevented the onset and progression of CRLMs by decreasing the formation of NETs. This preclinical evidence supports the potential use of anti-IL-11 antibodies to block the oncogenic signaling pathway in metastatic CRC.
Discussion
In this study, we elucidated the functional role of the tumor-secreted exosomal protein NID1 in influencing CRC progression and liver metastasis by analyzing exosomal proteins in metastatic CRC. Our findings revealed a dual mechanism by which EV-NID1 contributes to CRC metastasis. First, EV-NID1 altered the phenotype of CRC cells by modulating the expression of EMT-related genes, thereby enhancing the metastatic ability of these cells. Second, EV-NID1 induced the secretion of IL-11 by HSCs, which in turn activated neutrophils to form NETs in metastatic ecological niches. This NET formation facilitated the colonization and growth of CRC cells in the liver. Furthermore, our preclinical study demonstrated that blockade of the IL-11 signaling pathway with an IL-11 monoclonal antibody effectively inhibited the premetastatic effects mediated by EV-NID1, suggesting a promising strategy for intervention in CRLM (
Figure 7
G).
CRLM is one of the leading causes of mortality among patients with CRC and is driven primarily by the intricate interplay between tumor cells and the TME within the liver. Emerging evidence underscores the pivotal role of EVs in mediating intercellular communication and facilitating crosstalk between cancer cells and their microenvironment.
35
Notably, EVs enriched with microRNAs (miRNAs), particularly miRNA-rich EVs, have been implicated in promoting tumor metastasis across various cancer types.
36
,
37
Intriguingly, EVs not only harbor oncogenic miRNAs but also encompass tumor suppressor miRNAs, suggesting a complex regulatory landscape mediated by EV-associated miRNAs.
38
,
39
Although previous studies have shed light on the functional diversity of EV miRNAs, the functional potential of EV proteins in CRC remains inadequately understood. Further investigations are warranted to comprehensively understand the role of EV proteins in CRC and their contribution to disease progression and metastasis.
Through proteomic analysis, we identified NID1 as a protein enriched in EVs of metastatic CRC cells. NID1, also known as entactin, plays a crucial role as a structural component of the basement membrane and ECM. Its regulatory role in tumor metastasis has been extensively documented in various cancers, including breast, melanoma, ovarian, and endometrial cancers.
40
,
41
,
42
Despite accumulating evidence of the complex involvement of NID1 in different cancer types, its specific role in CRLM has remained elusive. Building upon previous research,
43
,
44
our study corroborates the findings that the exosomal protein NID1, which is secreted by metastatic CRC cells, enhances the metastatic potential of CRC cells. Furthermore, we revealed a function of the exosomal protein NID1 in modulating the premetastatic microenvironment of the liver, thereby facilitating CRLM by altering the hepatic immune microenvironment.
Interestingly, previous studies have implicated the involvement of the EV-NID1 protein in regulating the development of hepatocellular carcinoma in hepatocellular liver cancer.
19
However, the presence of NID1 in EVs from CRC cells represents a discovery in the context of CRC, suggesting that its role in intercellular communication during the development of liver metastasis in CRC remains poorly understood and warrants further investigation.
Liver metastasis in CRC is a multifaceted process involving intricate interactions between tumor cells and the TME, which play pivotal roles in metastasis and disease progression.
45
,
46
Various cellular and molecular components contribute to this complex process, highlighting the dynamic nature of CRLM.
Kupffer cells, as the resident macrophages of the liver, serve as the first line of defense against invading tumor cells and can influence tumor cell colonization and modulate the immune status through the secretion of factors.
47
,
48
,
49
Additionally, hematopoietic stem cells have emerged as key regulators that orchestrate and expedite metastatic progression by modulating the premetastatic niche and interacting with CRC cell recruitment during CRLM development.
22
Furthermore, once liver metastasis is established, the recruitment of neutrophils,
50
monocytes, and macrophages to the metastatic site further contributes to the complexity of the TME.
45
In response to cancer cell stimuli, HSCs release chemokines that promote tumor invasion and growth, underscoring their role in the metastatic process.
51
,
52
Understanding the mechanisms underlying stellate cell activation and metastasis to the liver holds promise for identifying therapeutic strategies for CRLM.
In our study, we demonstrated that highly metastatic CRC cell-derived EV-NID1 can activate HSCs, leading to the secretion of IL-11. IL-11, a member of the IL-6 family,
53
has unique functions, particularly in the liver, where IL11RA is highly expressed on HSCs, facilitating autocrine IL-11 activity.
54
Interestingly, IL-11 can directly act on HSCs via receptor binding in a paracrine or autocrine manner, as stimulated hematopoietic stem cells themselves secrete IL-11.
55
In vivo
experiments have shown that IL-11 can increase the number of neutrophils
56
,
57
,
58
and trigger the release of various inflammatory factors, including IL-8, IL-6, MCP1, CCL20, and CXCL1/5/6, which are crucial chemokines for neutrophil recruitment.
59
Furthermore, a monoclonal antibody targeting IL-11 (9MW3811) is currently undergoing clinical trials for tumor treatment, highlighting the therapeutic potential of targeting the IL-11 signaling pathway in CRLM management. These findings shed light on the intricate interplay between tumor cells, stromal cells, and immune cells in the liver microenvironment during CRLM, offering new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
In clinical practice, the efficacy of cilengitide, which targets integrin αv (ITGAV, CD51) in cancer therapy, has not met expectations,
60
,
61
underscoring the need to explore the underlying mechanisms of resistance to this target. Our study revealed that cilengitide was unable to fully counteract all the oncogenic effects induced by NID1 overexpression. This discovery reveals a previously unrecognized mechanism of action of cilengitide in tumor therapy, shedding light on potential reasons for its failure. Moreover, these findings support the translational potential of combination therapy targeting CD51 in the clinic.
NETs, which are abundant in metastatic tumors, play crucial roles in liver metastasis.
62
In our previous research, we demonstrated that inflammatory tumor-associated fibroblasts induced by FGF19 could promote the formation of NETs in CRLMs.
63
NETs release NET DNA, which acts as a chemokine to attract circulating tumor cells and enhance cell motility by binding to its receptor CCDC25.
62
Additionally, various factors, including cytokines, can activate neutrophils to produce NETs, accelerating the development and progression of liver metastases.
64
,
65
,
66
Our study proposes a regulatory mechanism for NETosis. We found that CRC-derived EV-NID1 promotes neutrophil aggregation and activation through the induction of IL-11 secretion from HSCs, leading to the formation of NET structures in the liver metastatic niche. Targeting tumor cells alone has been the conventional approach
67
,
68
in cancer treatment, but recent studies highlight the complexity and heterogeneity of the TME.
69
,
70
It may be more feasible to target the tumor-derived molecules responsible for inducing and maintaining the TME, including exosome-related factors.
In conclusion, our study validates the potential of EV-NID1 as a prognostic marker and therapeutic target in CRLM. Our preclinical findings support the use of anti-IL-11 therapy to target the IL-11 signaling pathway activated by EV-NID1-mediated HSC activation for the treatment of CRLM. Anti-IL-11 monoclonal antibodies are currently undergoing phase I clinical trials, supporting their potential as cancer therapeutic agents, particularly for patients with EV-NID1-mediated CRLM.
Limitations of the study
While this work establishes EV-NID1 as a mediator of CRLM through EMT induction and HSC-driven NET formation via IL-11, the reliance on human cell lines in immunocompromised murine models presents inherent constraints for dissecting immune mechanisms. The xenograft approach, though valuable for initial validation, limits our ability to fully characterize the complexity of human-specific immune interactions—particularly the nuanced crosstalk between HSCs, neutrophils, and other immune populations within an intact TME. Consequently, the precise immunological cascades linking IL-11 secretion to NETosis, as well as potential contributions from adaptive immunity, remain partially unresolved and warrant further investigation in immunocompetent or humanized models to strengthen clinical translatability.

Experimental model and study participant details
Serum collection
The primary cohort comprised 20 healthy donors and 70 CRC patients who underwent radical surgery at the 2nd Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University from January 2021 to April 2023. Fresh serum was obtained during surgery. Written consent was obtained from all patients before bile or serum collection.
CRC cohort and ethics
The primary CRC cohort consisted of patients who underwent surgical resection at the Cancer Hospital Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences from 2010 to 2018. Among them, 174 CRC patients were selected from the primary cohort if they met the following criteria: (I) underwent radical resection; (II) had formalin-immobilized tumor tissues, followed up, and had a complete medical history; (III) survived more than 30 days after surgery; and (IV) had no other malignancies. Tumor tissues were staged and classified according to the 8th edition AJCC/UICC TNM classification system. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Shanxi Provincial Cancer Hospital/Shanxi Hospital of the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences Cancer Hospital.
Cells and reagents
The human CRC cell lines SW480, KM12 and HCT116, the human colonic epithelial cell line NCM-460 and the hepatic stellate cell line LX-2 were obtained from the Chinese Academy of Sciences Cell Bank (Shanghai, China), authenticated by STR analysis and tested for mycoplasma contamination. SW480, HCT116 and KM12 cells were maintained in RPMI 1640 medium (Thermo Fisher), NCM-460 cells were maintained in DMEM/F-12 medium (Gibco) and LX-2 cells were maintained in MEM (Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Thermo Fisher) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin under 5% CO2 at 37°C.
In vivo
experiments
All the animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences (NCC2023A355). Six-week-old female BALB/c mice were purchased from Gempharmatech Laboratory (Nanjing, China). For spleen injection, after anesthesia, the spleens of the mice were removed via laparotomy. For the spleen injection, 2.5 × 106 CRC cells suspended in 50 μL of PBS were injected into the distal tip of the spleen with an insulin syringe (BD, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). A whitening bulge of the spleen was observed in the injection area. After the whitening bulge disappeared, the spleen was removed after ligation of the splenic vessels, and the abdominal wound was then sutured. The animals were maintained until death or until the end of the experiment. For intracardiac injections, the preparations used were similar to those used for splenic injections. After anesthesia, the location of the mouse heart was localized, 50 μL of PBS-suspended CRC cells were injected into the interior of the cardiac chambers using an insulin syringe, and arterial blood was withdrawn back to the heart prior to the injection to indicate the correct location. For cecum injection, 1 × 106 CRC cells suspended in 50 μL of matrix gel (Corning) dilution (matrix gel: PBS = 4:1) were injected into the plasma membrane layer of the cecum using an insulin syringe (BD, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). A whitening and bulging of the cecum was observed in the injection area upon successful injection, and then the abdominal wound was sutured. The animals were maintained until death or until the end of the experiment. A live imaging system (IVIS Spectrum; PerkinElmer) was used to detect
in vivo
metastases. Liver metastases were counted and confirmed by H&E staining.
For EV treatment, the mice were i.p. injected with 15 μg of EVs or with PBS as a control once per week for 3 weeks. For cilengitide and anti-IL-11 antibody treatment, the mice were i.p. injected with cilengitide (75 mg/kg, 5 times/week, HY-16141, Master of Bioactive Molecules) and an anti-IL-11 antibody (25 μg per mouse, MAB218, R&D Systems) every other day.
Stable clones of SW480 cells (5 × 106 cells) or SW480 cells (5 × 106 cells) overexpressing NID1 were injected subcutaneously into nude mice. Beginning on the third day after tumor cell injection, if necessary, EVs or cilengitide (75 mg/kg, 5 times/week) were injected every 3 days via intraperitoneal injection. Tumor diameters were measured with an external caliper every 3 days. The tumor volume (V) was calculated according to the following formula: volume (mm3) = (length×width2)/2. After 18/21 days, the tumors were removed, photographed and weighed.

Method details
Exosome isolation
Exosomes were isolated from serum and CRC medium via differential centrifugation. In brief, serum and Exo-depleted–fetal bovine serum media were centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 30 min at 4°C. The impurities, cellular sediment, and debris were removed, and the supernatant was ultracentrifuged at 110,000 × g for 70 min at 4°C. After that, the pellets were resuspended in PBS and ultracentrifuged again at 110,000 × g for 70 min at 4°C. The final pellets, which were mainly Exosomes, were resuspended and resuspended in PBS.
Patient-derived organoids
Freshly resected CRC tissues were minced into 0.5–1 mm3 pieces. The supernatants, including any blood cells and floating pieces of fat, were discarded. After incubation in IV collagenase (Sigma‒Aldrich) for 30 min, the tissues were passed through 70-μm filter gauze and centrifuged at 300 × g for 5 min at 4°C. After the removal of the supernatant, Matrigel (R&D, Minnesota, USA) and expansion medium were proportionally mixed with the pellets and seeded in 24-well plates. The organoids were incubated for 10–15 days in Bowel cancer organoid medium (Mogengel Biotechnology) supplemented with 1% penicillin/streptomycin.The collection of all samples was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University (Approval No. KY2024-176).
Tissue microarray and IHC
Typical paraffin-embedded sections of CRC tissues were used for TMA construction and immunohistochemistry (IHC) scoring after hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining to confirm the histological features of all samples by a senior pathologist. For the TMA construct, a 1.5 mm diameter core biopsy sample was extracted from each.
Sample and placed on a TMA slide
For IHC, slides were pretreated in EDTA buffer (pH 9.0) or sodium citrate buffer (pH 6.0) for antigen retrieval. Primary anti-PTPN9 antibody (1:50), anti-
p
-FGFR2 antibody (1:100) and anti-ACAP1 antibody (1:100) were used and incubated at 4°C overnight. Rabbit anti-goat and goat anti-rabbit antibodies labeled with biotin (Zsbio, Beijing, China) were used at room temperature for 30 min. The peroxidase reaction was carried out with 3,3′-diaminobenzidine solution (Coolaber).
The stained slides were screened with a slide scanner (Pannoramic MIDI; 3DHISTECH, Budapest, Hungary). The tumor area was selected by senior pathologists, and the IHC results were quantified using Quant Center software. The area of each area of staining was calculated, and the staining intensity was classified as weak, medium, or strong. IHC score = (percentage of weak intensity×1) + (percentage of medium intensity×2) + (percentage of strong intensity×3). The cohort was divided into different groups on the basis of the cutoff value of the IHC score, which was identified as the point where the sum of specificity and sensitivity was the highest in the receiver operating characteristic curve.
PKH67 fluorescent labeling
Purified exosomes were labeled with PKH67 fluorescence (Sigma). Exosomes were resuspended in 100 μL of diluent C and then mixed with 100 μL of diluent C containing 5 μL of PKH67 dye solution (4 × 10−6M). After PKH67 staining, the exosomes were washed in PBS and collected by ultracentrifugation (110,000 × g for 70 min) at 4°C to remove the free dye.
Transmission electron microscopy
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was used to observe exosome morphology. The purified exosomes were dropped on a copper grid and observed via transmission electron microscopy (FEI Tecnai Spirit TEM T12, Thermo Scientific) at 80 kV.
Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and NanoFCM
The exosome particle size was measured via nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) using a ZetaView PMX 110 (Particle Metrix, Meerbusch, Germany), and nanoflow was measured using N30E (NanoFCM, Xiamen, China). The purified exosomes were diluted 1:200 in PBS and subjected to NTA or NanoFCM. Each sample was measured in triplicate. Exosome numbers and size distributions were analyzed using Zetaview.
Cell proliferation assay
CCK-8 assays were performed to assess cell proliferation. Briefly, the cells were plated into 96-well plates (3 × 103 cells/well) and incubated for 4 days. A total of 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent (Dojindo, Kumamoto, Japan) was added each day, and the mixture was incubated at 37°C for 1 h. The absorbance value at 450 nm was detected using a spectrophotometer (Molecular Devices Company, France).
Transwell assay
To detect changes in cell migration and invasion, a transwell assay was performed using 24-well plates with chambers (Corning Inc., 8.0-μm pore size) with/without Matrigel precoating. A total of 5 × 104 SW480 cells or 1 × 105 KM12 cells were seeded into the upper chambers (diluted 1:6 with serum-free medium). Approximately 500 μL of complete medium supplemented with 20% FBS was added to the lower chamber. After incubation for 24 h, the cells on the lower side of the chamber were fixed with methanol and stained with 0.5% crystal violet (Solarbio) for 30 min. The cells were counted in three random fields at 200× magnification.
Mass spectrometry
Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC‒MS/MS) was performed by OEbiotech Company. On-line chromatographic separation was performed on an Easy nLC 1200 system (Thermo Fisher). Data Related Acquisition (DDA) MS was used to collect series of MS data on a ThermoFisher Q Exactive mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher, USA) equipped with a Nano-Flex ion source.
RNA sequencing
Total mRNA was extracted from SW480, SW480-LM3 and LX-2 cells using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen). The RNA was sequenced via an Illumina HiSeq 4000 (LC-Bio Technologies). Clean reads were separately aligned to the reference genome in orientation mode using TopHat software. The sequence reads were mapped to the reference genome using HISAT2 software. The transcript abundances (read counts) were estimated with StringTie. Normalization and differential expression analysis of mRNAs were conducted using DESeq2 in the R package.
Quantitative real-time PCR
TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) was used to separate total mRNA from frozen CRC cell lines according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The RNA quality was subsequently determined via a NanoDrop system (Thermo Fisher). The purified RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using a high-capacity cDNA reverse transcription kit (TOYOBO, Japan), and RT‒qPCR was performed using SYBR Green master mix (Roche, Switzerland). The relative expression levels of the target genes were calculated using the 2-ΔΔCt method, and GAPDH was used as an internal control. All primers were designed using Primer Express version 5.0 software (Applied Biosystems, USA).
Immunofluorescence assay
The cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min and incubated in Tween 20 for cell membrane perforation. The cells were incubated in 5% goat serum to block nonspecific antigen binding for 30 min and then incubated with primary antibodies against NID1 (1:100), IL-11 (1:100) and Destin (1:100) for 12 h at 4°C. The secondary antibodies goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 594 (Invitrogen, Cat # A-21207) and anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 488 (Invitrogen, Cat # A-21202) were used to immerse the cells for 1 h at room temperature. Nuclei were stained with DAPI (Thermo Fisher), and images were taken with a confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss, LSM880). The Pearson coefficient was analyzed with Image-Pro Plus.
Immunofluorescence of paraffin-embedded tissues
Immunofluorescence (IF) staining was performed as previously described.

After antigen retrieval and antigen blocking, the sections were incubated with diluted primary antibodies against MPO (1:50), H3Cit (1:200), and IL-11 (1:100) at 4°C overnight. Western blotting
Total protein was extracted using radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) lysis buffer (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) supplemented with 1% PMSF (Beyotime) and 1% phosphatase inhibitor (Solarbio, Beijing, China). Proteins were separated via 10% SDS‒PAGE after denaturation and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. Primary antibodies against CD63 (1:1,000), TSG-101 (1:1,000), calnexin (1:1,000), NID1 (1:1,000), E-cadherin (1:1,000), N-cadherin (1:1,000), Snail (1:1,000), vimentin (1:1,000), ZEB1 (1:1,000), and IL-11 (1:1,000) and corresponding secondary antibodies were used. The signal was detected via enhanced chemiluminescence (Millipore).
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
The IL-6, IL-8, IL-11 and TIMP2 concentrations in the LX-2 culture medium were measured by ELISA using the hIL-6 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04638h), hIL-8 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04641h), hIL-11 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04596h) and TIMP2 kit (CUSABIO Cat. No. CSB-E04733h) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The ELISA absorbance values were read on a BIOTEK spectrophotometer (Vermont, USA) at 450 nm.
Construction of the NID1 expression plasmid
To increase the expression level of NID1, we amplified the human NID1 gene from cDNA by PCR and cloned it into the pLenti-EF1a lentiviral vector (GeneChem, China). In addition, to express NID1 in cellular EVs, the NID1 fragment was cloned and inserted into the CMV-XP-MCS-EF1-Puro cloning lentiviral vector (System Biosciences) using XPack EV Protein Engineering Technology (System Biosciences). NID1 was expressed through XPack EV Protein Engineering Technology (System Biosciences) for expression in the EVs of HCT116 and NCM-460 cells. The extracellular vesicle (EV) purification process was performed as described above. The purified EV-NID1 and control EVs were resuspended in Exo-depleted–fetal bovine serum media for further use. To inhibit exosome secretion, donor cells were treated with GW4869 (MedChemExpress) for 48 h. The conditioned medium was then collected, and EVs were isolated using the ultracentrifugation method described above. The GW4869-treated EV fraction was subsequently incubated with recipient colorectal cancer cells under the same conditions.
Overexpression and knockdown
To increase the expression level of NID1, the human NID1 gene was amplified from cDNA via PCR and subsequently cloned and inserted into the pcDNA3.1 or pLenti-EF1a lentiviral vector (GeneChem, China). Short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) and the packaging plasmids GV, pHelper1.0 and pHelper2.0 were used for knockdown.
Cytokine antibody array
Cytokines were detected in the media of LX-2 cells stimulated with EV-NID1 using the Human Inflammation Array C3 Kit (AAH-INF-3-2, RayBiotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, LX-2 cells were stimulated with EV-NID1 for 72 h. The culture supernatants were collected, centrifuged at 1,000 × g to discard the pellets and 10 × concentrated with Amicon Ultra15 mL filters (10 kDa, Millipore) at 4,000 × g. Array membranes, previously spotted with capture antibodies by the manufacturer, were incubated with 1 mL of culture supernatants overnight at 4°C. After being washed three times, the membranes were incubated with streptavidin-HRP for 30 min and visualized with Chemi-Reagent Mix. The protein signal was detected with a chemifluorescence detection system (Amersham Imager 600, GE). Quantitative analysis of specific protein expression was performed using ImageJ.

Statistical analysis
SPSS 22.0 (IBM, Chicago, Illinois, USA) and GraphPad Prism 6.0 (GraphPad Software, CA, USA) were used for statistical analysis. The correlations between NID1 expression and clinicopathological features were evaluated via the chi-square test. The Kaplan‒Meier method was used to plot survival curves, and the log rank test was used to analyze the statistical significance. The “survival” R package in RStudio software was used to calculate Harrell’s concordance index (C-index), which measures the proportion of pairs for which the predicted and observed outcomes are concordant. Multivariate analysis with a Cox regression model was performed to compare independent prognostic factors. A paired
